items.label: f02-stale-dashboard
items.front: Why did Recall's dashboard keep showing '40d' after the user skipped five days, and what fixed it?
items.back: It displayed stats.currentStreak as stored, and the streak was only recomputed on grading — stored state is not current truth. main shows effectiveStreak, computed at read time, in loadDashboard.

items.label: f03-test-time-code
items.front: How does Recall make its date and streak logic testable, and what kind of test found the DST bug?
items.back: Every function in dates.ts and streak.ts takes now and tz as arguments, so no fake timers are needed. A property test across every IANA zone (example tests only cover known edge cases) pinned the DST-at-midnight failures.

items.label: f01-lost-update-shape
items.front: What is the 'lost update' shape in Recall's original gradeCard, and how do you prevent it without locks?
items.back: Read-compute-write with the reads outside the atomic batch and no lock or version check, so two tabs both read reps = 0 and both write. Prevent it with optimistic concurrency: put a version column (reps) in the UPDATE's WHERE and treat zero rows as a conflict; move computation into SQL (xp = xp + n) where possible.

items.prompt: Recall's first gradeCard sent its three writes in one atomic db.batch. Why could a retried grade still graduate a new card from Learning to Review?

choices.text: Atomic is not idempotent: a retry after a lost response re-read the updated state and graded it a second time
The XP increment ran outside the batch and double-counted
FSRS treats every second grade on a card as Easy
Neon split the batch into separate transactions under load

choices: Atomic is not idempotent: a retry after a lost response re-read the updated state and graded it a second time
The XP increment ran outside the batch and double-counted
FSRS treats every second grade on a card as Easy
Neon split the batch into separate transactions under load

items.explanation: 'Atomic means the writes commit together or not at all. Idempotent means doing the operation twice has the same effect as doing it once.' A new card graded Good twice goes from Learning (+10 min) to Review (+4 days).

items.prompt: Why did the original startOfLocalDayUTC('2026-09-06', 'America/Santiago') return 23:00 on Sept 5 local time?

choices.text: Date.UTC rounds negative offsets toward the previous day
Santiago's tz database entry was missing from Node's Intl data
DST starts at midnight there, so local 00:00 does not exist and the two offset passes landed in the previous day
The function used the server's local zone instead of tz

choices: Date.UTC rounds negative offsets toward the previous day
Santiago's tz database entry was missing from Node's Intl data
DST starts at midnight there, so local 00:00 does not exist and the two offset passes landed in the previous day
The function used the server's local zone instead of tz

items.explanation: In zones where DST begins at 00:00 'local midnight isn't a real instant'; main steps forward an hour at a time (at most 3) while the local day is still before dayISO.

items.prompt: A user reviews in Tokyo in the morning, then switches Settings to Los Angeles (still yesterday there) and grades a card. What does applyActivity on main do?

choices.text: Resets the streak to 1, since the gap is not 1 or 2
Throws, because lastActivityDate is after today
Adds 1 to the streak and spends the weekly freeze
Returns the stats unchanged, because a gap of zero or less is treated as the same day

choices: Resets the streak to 1, since the gap is not 1 or 2
Throws, because lastActivityDate is after today
Adds 1 to the streak and spends the weekly freeze
Returns the stats unchanged, because a gap of zero or less is treated as the same day

items.explanation: The original code reset on any gap not 0, 1 or 2, including negative gaps (a 40-day streak came back as 1). main returns stats unchanged when gap <= 0 (streak.ts:44).

items.prompt: On main, two tabs grade the same card within a second, both sending expectedReps 0. What happens to the second grade?

choices.text: The second grade waits on a row lock and then applies on top
Its conditional UPDATE matches no row because reps is now 1, so it returns stale without logging or adding XP
Both grades apply, producing two review_logs rows and double XP
The second grade overwrites the first, since last writer wins

choices: The second grade waits on a row lock and then applies on top
Its conditional UPDATE matches no row because reps is now 1, so it returns stale without logging or adding XP
Both grades apply, producing two review_logs rows and double XP
The second grade overwrites the first, since last writer wins

items.explanation: The UPDATE's WHERE includes reps = expectedReps (and the card still active); zero rows returned means { stale: true, reason: 'reps' }, and only after a row is returned does the log + XP batch run.

items.prompt: Why does Recall use db.batch rather than db.transaction for its writes, and what is the cost?

choices.text: db.transaction is deprecated in Drizzle; the cost is no rollback
Batches allow retries; the cost is duplicate review logs
db.batch is faster on Postgres; the cost is losing atomicity
neon-http cannot hold an interactive transaction; the cost is that no statement can depend on another's result

choices: db.transaction is deprecated in Drizzle; the cost is no rollback
Batches allow retries; the cost is duplicate review logs
db.batch is faster on Postgres; the cost is losing atomicity
neon-http cannot hold an interactive transaction; the cost is that no statement can depend on another's result

items.explanation: 'db.batch instead of db.transaction, forced by neon-http... the cost is that no statement can depend on another statement's result.' Data-modifying CTEs are the escape hatch.

items.prompt: Why does Recall store last_activity_date as a YYYY-MM-DD calendar day rather than a timestamp it re-derives the day from?

choices.text: Postgres cannot index timestamptz columns efficiently
Deriving the day from a timestamp would let a time-zone change rewrite history
FSRS requires calendar days for its due-date math
Strings are smaller, which keeps the Neon bill down

choices: Postgres cannot index timestamptz columns efficiently
Deriving the day from a timestamp would let a time-zone change rewrite history
FSRS requires calendar days for its due-date math
Strings are smaller, which keeps the Neon bill down

items.explanation: 'Rejected: storing last_activity as a timestamp and deriving the day each time, because then changing the zone would rewrite history.' Days as strings also avoid DST-hour day arithmetic.

items.prompt: A streak computes 'today' as new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10). A Los Angeles user reviews at 6 pm. What goes wrong?

choices.text: It is already the next UTC day, so the review counts toward tomorrow's streak day
The review counts for yesterday, because LA is ahead of UTC
The slice returns the time instead of the date after 6 pm
Nothing, because toISOString uses the server's local zone

choices: It is already the next UTC day, so the review counts toward tomorrow's streak day
The review counts for yesterday, because LA is ahead of UTC
The slice returns the time instead of the date after 6 pm
Nothing, because toISOString uses the server's local zone

items.explanation: toISOString is UTC; 6 pm PDT is 01:00 UTC the next day. 'today' is a business concept defined by the user's time zone, not the server clock.

items.prompt: In the user_stats upsert, why is the xp column safe under concurrent grades while the streak columns are safe only by coincidence?

choices.text: xp is written first in the batch, so it always wins the race
streak columns are recomputed nightly, so races are corrected later
xp is stored as a bigint, while streaks are stored as strings
xp is incremented inside the database, while streak values were computed from a stale read and written last-writer-wins

choices: xp is written first in the batch, so it always wins the race
streak columns are recomputed nightly, so races are corrected later
xp is stored as a bigint, while streaks are stored as strings
xp is incremented inside the database, while streak values were computed from a stale read and written last-writer-wins

items.explanation: xp uses sql`${userStats.xp} + ${xpEarned}`, an atomic increment; streak fields are values from a stale read, safe only because same-day concurrent grades compute identical values.

choices.text: Server actions reject retried requests with the same payload
Retries need the idempotency key to choose an exponential backoff
Retries without idempotency exceed Neon's HTTP rate limit
A naive retry after a committed-but-lost response re-grades the card and moves its schedule forward

items.explanation: 'Any future retry on failure code, added naively, re-grades and graduates the card... This is why idempotency has to come before retries.'

choices.text: The retry throws, so the client discards the card permanently
The retry is applied again, but XP is deduplicated by the batch
The retry succeeds idempotently via a client_review_id key
Nothing is double-counted, but the retry comes back stale so the session summary misses that grade's XP
